short: First law of thermodynamics: change in internal energy = Q − W.
long: The first law states that the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat supplied to it minus the work done by it: ΔU = Q − W.
trick: Q − W (heat in minus work out) is the fixed form of the first law — memorize it exactly, since the other forms (Q/W, W/Q, 1+Q/W) don't represent any standard physical law.

options.a: Wrong — dividing heat by work isn't a meaningful physical relationship for internal energy change.
options.b: Wrong — same issue, inverted division.
options.c: Correct — ΔU = Q − W is the first law of thermodynamics.
options.d: Wrong — not a standard form of the first law.

short: Rejecting 1/4 of absorbed heat gives 75% efficiency (η = 1 − 1/4).
long: Efficiency η = 1 − (heat rejected/heat absorbed). If the engine rejects one-fourth of the heat taken in, then η = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 = 75%.
trick: Efficiency is always 1 minus the FRACTION of heat rejected (not the fraction converted to work directly, though they end up being complementary) — a quick way to compute efficiency from rejected-heat fractions.

options.a: Wrong — 100% efficiency is impossible per the second law (some heat must always be rejected).
options.b: Wrong — would require rejecting half the heat, not a quarter.
options.c: Wrong — would require rejecting three-quarters of the heat, not a quarter.
options.d: Correct — rejecting 1/4 of the heat gives 75% efficiency.

short: Under adiabatic conditions (Q=0), the first law reduces to W = −ΔU.
long: Adiabatic means no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (Q=0). The first law ΔU=Q−W then becomes ΔU=−W, or equivalently W=−ΔU — the work done comes entirely at the expense of (or contributes entirely to) the internal energy.
trick: Adiabatic ⇒ Q=0 ⇒ the first law simplifies immediately to W=−ΔU (or ΔU=−W) — a frequently tested thermodynamics shortcut.

options.a: Wrong — Q=W would apply to an isothermal process, not an adiabatic one.
options.b: Wrong — this doesn't reflect Q=0 being substituted into the first law correctly.
options.c: Wrong — Q=ΔU would require W=0, not the general adiabatic case.
options.d: Correct — W=−ΔU follows directly from setting Q=0 in the first law.

short: The NOT gate symbol is a triangle with a small bubble (inversion circle) at its output.
long: In digital logic, a NOT gate (inverter) is drawn as a triangle pointing in the direction of signal flow, with a small circle ('bubble') at the output tip indicating logical inversion.
trick: That small output bubble is the universal symbol for 'inverted' across all logic gate diagrams — a NAND is just an AND with that same bubble added, a NOR is an OR with the bubble added, and so on.

options.a: Correct — triangle with an output bubble is the standard NOT gate symbol.
options.b: Wrong — the AND gate has a distinct flat-front, rounded-back shape without an inversion bubble.
options.c: Wrong — the OR gate has a curved, pointed shape without an inversion bubble.
options.d: Wrong — a diode symbol isn't a logic gate at all.

short: The X-plate voltage in a CRO is supplied by a time base generator.
long: In a cathode ray oscilloscope, the horizontal (X) deflection is driven by a time base generator, which produces a sawtooth voltage that sweeps the beam steadily across the screen to represent the passage of time.
trick: X-plates = time base (horizontal sweep representing time); Y-plates = the actual input signal being measured (vertical deflection) — always pair X with 'time', Y with 'signal'.

options.a: Wrong — an audio generator produces sound-frequency signals, not the CRO's time-sweep voltage.
options.b: Wrong — a signal generator produces the input waveform being studied (typically fed to the Y-plates), not the X-plate sweep.
options.c: Correct — the time base generator specifically drives the X-plates.
options.d: Wrong — 'linear generator' isn't the standard named component for this function.

short: Doubling area and halving separation quadruples capacitance (C ∝ A/d).
long: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor: C = ε₀A/d. Doubling A and halving d: new C = ε₀(2A)/(d/2) = 4 × (ε₀A/d) = 4C — the capacitance becomes four times larger.
trick: C ∝ A/d — any change to A and d compounds multiplicatively: doubling A doubles C, and separately halving d doubles C again, so together they quadruple it.

options.a: Wrong — both changes affect capacitance; it doesn't stay the same.
options.b: Correct — doubling A and halving d together give a factor of 4 increase.
options.c: Wrong — underestimates the combined effect of both changes together.
options.d: Wrong — this would happen only if d were doubled (not halved) while A stayed fixed — the opposite of what's described.

short: Energy stored: ½CV² = ½(1×10⁻⁶)(10²) = 50×10⁻⁶ J = 0.05 mJ.
long: Energy stored in a charged capacitor: E = ½CV² = ½(1×10⁻⁶ F)(10 V)² = ½(1×10⁻⁶)(100) = 50×10⁻⁶ J = 50 μJ = 0.05 mJ.
trick: Watch your final unit conversion carefully: 50 μJ (micro) equals 0.05 mJ (milli), since 1 mJ = 1000 μJ — easy to misplace a decimal point here.

options.a: Wrong — off by a factor of 10 from the correct value.
options.b: Wrong — off by a factor of 100 from the correct value.
options.c: Correct — 0.05 mJ matches the ½CV² calculation.
options.d: Wrong — off by a factor of 1000 from the correct value.

short: A junction diode's I-V curve is markedly asymmetric — negligible current for reverse bias, sharply rising current for forward bias beyond a threshold.
long:
A real diode conducts easily in forward bias (current rises steeply once the voltage exceeds a small threshold, roughly 0.6-0.7V for silicon) but blocks current almost entirely in reverse bias — producing a distinctly nonlinear, asymmetric curve rather than a straight or gently-curved line through the origin.

**Note:** based on the diagram descriptions transcribed alongside this question, option A's description ('near-zero current for negative V, rising sharply for positive V') more closely matches a diode's well-known asymmetric characteristic curve than option B's description ('roughly linear through the origin'), which sounds closer to an ohmic (resistor-like) response. Left as the source's marked answer since the original diagram isn't independently viewable here to confirm which lettered option it actually corresponds to — flagged for a possible mismatch between the answer key and the diagram transcription.
trick: A diode's I-V curve is famously asymmetric and nonlinear (steep rise only past a forward threshold voltage, near-zero for reverse bias) — very different from a straight-line (ohmic/resistor) response.

options.a: Based on the diagram description, this shape more closely matches a real diode's known asymmetric behaviour — though not the source's marked answer.
options.b: Marked correct in the source, though its 'roughly linear' description reads more like an ohmic (resistor) response than a diode's characteristic curve — see note above.
options.c: Wrong — a perfectly straight line through the origin describes an ohmic resistor, not a diode.
options.d: Wrong — disconnected segments don't match a diode's continuous (if steeply curved) I-V relationship.
